AdjudicationRule.description: A single adjudication rule with conditions and an action.

action.description: Disposition to assign when this rule matches. This also decides how the rule matches a multi-charge item. A rule matches an item if ANY one of its charges satisfies the conditions, UNLESS it is more lenient than the rule set's `default_action`, or its action is `clear` at equal rank — those must be satisfied by EVERY charge. Flagging one bad charge out of many is accuracy; clearing an item on the strength of one benign charge is not. An equal-rank `review` or `consider` rule matches on ANY charge so that it can name itself as the specific reason rather than yielding to the default.

An equal-rank `review` or `consider` rule matches on ANY charge so that it can name itself as the specific reason rather than yielding to the default. AdverseActionCancelledPayload.description:
Fired when an adverse action is cancelled before finalization.

Three dispatchers fire this event — the platform route
(``api/v1/adverse_actions.py::cancel_adverse_action``), the admin
route (``api/v1/admin/adverse_actions.py::cancel_adverse_action``),
and the lifecycle transition
(``services/adverse_action/lifecycle.py::cancel_adverse_action``).

All three call the shared assembler
:func:`gonos.services.webhook_service.assemble_adverse_action_cancelled_payload`
(#1032), so the wire shape is byte-identical across dispatchers.
Historically the three dispatchers sent disjoint keys — the two
API routes sent ``{aa_id, status}`` and the lifecycle path sent
``{aa_id, cancelled_at}`` — and the allowlist admitted
``{aa_id, cancelled_at, cancellation_reason}``. Net result: the two
API-route receivers got ``{aa_id}`` only (``status`` stripped), the
lifecycle receiver got ``{aa_id, cancelled_at}``, and
``cancellation_reason`` was a dead promise nobody populated.

The ``AdverseAction`` model has no ``cancelled_at`` column, so each
dispatcher stamps ``datetime.now(UTC)`` at dispatch time.

adverse_action_id.description: ID of the cancelled adverse action record
adverse_action_id.title: Adverse Action Id

cancelled_at.description: ISO 8601 timestamp of when the cancellation was dispatched. Stamped synchronously by every dispatcher because the ``AdverseAction`` model has no ``cancelled_at`` column. Newly delivered by the two API-route dispatchers as of 2026-08-15 (previously sent only by the lifecycle path).
cancelled_at.title: Cancelled At

idempotency_key.description: Deterministic dedup key of the form ``adverse_action.cancelled:<adverse_action_id>``. Receivers can safely dedupe replays on this value. Matches the convention set by ``adverse_action.completed`` (#993).
idempotency_key.title: Idempotency Key

organization_id.description: ID of the organization that owns the resource
organization_id.title: Organization Id

status.description: Adverse action status at cancellation — always the string ``'cancelled'`` in production. Newly delivered by all three dispatchers as of 2026-08-15 (previously stripped from the wire on the two API-route dispatchers by the allowlist, and not sent at all by the lifecycle path).
status.title: Status

timestamp.description: ISO 8601 timestamp of when the event was emitted
timestamp.title: Timestamp

AdverseActionCancelledPayload.title: AdverseActionCancelledPayload

AdverseActionConsumerResponse.description:
Audit-round-9 adverse-action H5 fix: consumer-facing response.

The platform-facing ``AdverseActionResponse`` strips
``credit_score_disclosure`` because credit scores are
consumer-confidential and the platform integrator should not see
them. The previous implementation reused ``AdverseActionResponse``
on consumer endpoints too, hiding the credit score disclosure from
the consumer themselves — a §1681m(a)(2) and §1681g(f) violation (ADR 0095)
(the consumer has the right to see the credit score used in the
adverse decision).

This subclass overrides the parent validator so credit_score_disclosure
survives serialization for consumer endpoints. ``adverse_reasons`` is
still extracted to the top-level field for convenience.

Phase-3 adds consumer-facing waiting-period visibility (Gap 6a):
``pre_notice_delivered`` and ``business_days_remaining`` so the consumer
can see where they are in the §1681m(a) waiting period.

adverse_reasons: Criminal record found in background check

assessment_factors.description: EEOC individualized assessment factors. Required when ``individualized_assessment_required=True`` and the decision is 'deny'. Three fields are mandatory and each must contain a substantive narrative (no empty placeholder strings): ``nature_of_offense`` (≥5 chars, nature and gravity), ``time_elapsed`` (≥3 chars, time since the offense), ``job_relatedness`` (≥5 chars, how the record relates to the specific job duties). ``additional_context`` is optional and captures mitigating / aggravating factors. None until the assessment has been recorded.

AssessmentFactorsSchema.description:
Typed schema for individualized assessment factors.

Supports both employment context (EEOC guidance) and tenant-screening
context (HUD 2016 guidance on criminal history in tenancy decisions).

EEOC requires consideration of: (1) nature/gravity of offense, (2) time
elapsed since offense, (3) job-relatedness of the record.

HUD 2016 guidance for tenant screening requires the same first two,
plus a "relevance to tenancy suitability" analysis (instead of job-
relatedness). Operators populate ``tenancy_relevance`` for tenant
screening adverse actions and ``job_relatedness`` for employment ones.
Exactly one of the two relevance fields must be set.

additional_context.description: Any additional mitigating or aggravating context considered
additional_context.title: Additional Context

assessed_by.description: Name or email of the operator who performed the assessment. Captured for accountability and audit trail.
assessed_by.title: Assessed By

assessed_risk.description: Operator's categorical risk rating after individualized assessment. Optional; useful for audit defense and disparate-impact analysis.
assessed_risk.title: Assessed Risk

job_relatedness.description: Employment context (EEOC): how the record relates to the specific job duties (e.g., 'driving record relevant for delivery driver role'). Required for employment adverse actions; leave null for tenant screening.
job_relatedness.title: Job Relatedness

nature_of_offense.description: Nature and gravity of the offense or record (e.g., 'felony assault')
nature_of_offense.title: Nature Of Offense

tenancy_relevance.description: Tenant-screening context (HUD 2016 guidance): how the record relates to tenancy suitability (e.g., 'recent property-damage conviction relevant to lease compliance'). Required for tenant-screening adverse actions; leave null for employment.
tenancy_relevance.title: Tenancy Relevance

time_elapsed.description: Time elapsed since the offense or conduct (e.g., '3 years since conviction')
time_elapsed.title: Time Elapsed

AuditLogResponse.description: Typed response for audit log entries.

action.description: What happened, as `<resource>.<verb>` (`check.created`, `dispute.extended`). **Not an enum**: the set grows with each release and the `action` filter accepts any string, so match on the values you care about rather than exhausting them. An action is **not** a unique key for a row — one request can write two rows under the same action, distinguished only by `details` (see below). A `.reason` or `.statement` suffix is not a sub-event: it marks a platform-scope row carrying a consumer's own free text, readable only by CRA staff through `GET /admin/platform/audit-logs`. Those rows are never returned by the organization-scoped audit endpoints.
action.title: Action

actor_id.description: Identifier of the actor, interpreted according to `actor_type`. For `actor_type=platform` this is USUALLY the ORGANIZATION id, not a per-key identity — two API keys belonging to one organization are indistinguishable here. A small number of platform-staff actions record the operator instead (`report.approved`, `adverse_action.pre_notice_delivery_override`, which can also record the literal `unknown`), so check `action` before resolving this against your own roster.
actor_id.title: Actor Id

actor_type.description:
Who acted. One of `admin`, `consumer`, `organization`, `platform`, `scim`, `service`, `system`, `unknown`, `user` — the same set the `actor_type` query filter enumerates.

**Not a filter for 'everything my API key did.'** One request authenticated with an organization API key writes rows under more than one value: `platform` at the API layer, and `system` from the shared service layer beneath it — including the row that records a dispute deadline actually moving. A few routes record `organization` instead (the `furnisher.*` actions). To reconstruct one request, group by `correlation_id`, not by `actor_type`.
actor_type.title: Actor Type

correlation_id.description: Groups the rows written by one request. Always a UUID or null: a non-UUID `X-Correlation-ID` is echoed on the response headers but cannot land here, because the middleware resolves a separate UUID for this column — so sending a junk header does not make your own actions uncorrelatable. Null on rows written outside a request context, and on some service-layer rows that do not yet receive it.
correlation_id.title: Correlation Id

details.description: Action-specific payload. **An open object with no schema**, so `make api-diff` cannot see changes to it and they do not appear as breaking changes — treat every key as optional and check before reading. Keys vary by action AND by writer: one call to `POST /disputes/{id}/request-extension` produces two `dispute.extension_requested` rows, one carrying `reason` and one carrying `reason_recorded`, and `details` is the only field that tells them apart.
details.title: Details

id.description: Monotonic row id, and the tiebreaker you want when ordering. `timestamp` is transaction-granular — every row written by one request carries the SAME value — so `timestamp` alone does not order the rows within a request; `id` does.
id.title: Id

ip_address.description: Client IP of the originating request. Null for rows a background worker or a service call wrote, which have no request context.
ip_address.title: Ip Address

resource_id.description: Id of the affected resource, in the namespace `resource_type` names.
resource_id.title: Resource Id

resource_type.description: Type of the affected resource; pair with `resource_id` to filter.
resource_type.title: Resource Type

timestamp.description: When the transaction that recorded the event began, UTC. Not per-row: rows written by one request share a timestamp, so sort by `id` to order them (see `id`).
timestamp.title: Timestamp

verified.title: Verified

AuditProseEntry.description:
A retained consumer-authored dispute-prose row visible to §1681g.

ADR 0101 / ADR 0102. `_record_reason_for_cra_only` writes
platform-scope `AuditLog` rows that the FCRA requires the CRA to
retain (§1681e(a), §1681i(c)). These rows survive consumer-driven
erasure under §1798.145(d)'s FCRA exemption. Under §1681g(a)(1) the
consumer is entitled to see them.

This entry projects a single such row. Only consumer-authored rows
appear here per ADR 0102 Provisional; the org-typed and CRA-staff
rows are the open question on #2319.

`prose` is served verbatim from the stored row. ADR 0064's
sanitization may have rewritten patterns (bare 9-digit runs, ISO
dates) at write time, so the string may be an altered copy of the
consumer's original words. Marking that transformation is #2382
part 2.

kind.description: Which kind of consumer prose this row carries. One of: 'statement_contest' (a §1681i(a)(3)(B) frivolous-contest resubmission), 'statement_amended' (a new §1681i(b) consumer statement that replaced an earlier one), 'statement_superseded' (the earlier statement an amendment replaced — retained because §1681e(a) procedures retention applies), 'accommodation_reason' (the consumer's own account of why they need a §1681i(a)(1)(B) extension, re-supplied after an encryption failure).
kind.title: Kind

prose.description: The consumer's own words from the row, as stored. If ``was_sanitized`` is true, ADR 0064's sanitiser rewrote at least one PII pattern in the string before persistence; the exact bytes the consumer typed are not recoverable, but the shape (what the sentence is about) is preserved. If false, the prose is verbatim — or the row predates the #2382 part 2 sanitiser-marker and verbatim-ness cannot be asserted.
prose.title: Prose

was_sanitized.description: True when the audit sanitiser (ADR 0064) rewrote PII patterns in this row's stored prose before persistence (ADR 0101 §3 / ADR 0102 / #2382 part 2). Rows written before this marker shipped read as false regardless — the signal is forward-only.
was_sanitized.title: Was Sanitized

CandidateResponse.description:
Candidate record as returned by the API.

R21-10: ssn_last_four is redacted in API responses to prevent
exposure of PII through list/detail endpoints.

Audience-typed under ADR 0011 / #1608: `__audience__ = "org"` because
the six routes returning this class (`api/v1/candidates.py:221,864,
936,1076` and `api/v1/admin/candidates.py:32,228`) all serve the
organization. `CandidateConsumerResponse` below overrides
`__audience__ = "consumer"` for the one consumer surface that projects
a candidate through this hierarchy.

ADR 0014 (Option B): `accommodation_requested` is a §12112(d)-adjacent
disability signal — values name specific accommodations
(`screen_reader`, `interpreter`, etc.). The org receives a fact-only
`has_accommodation: bool` computed from the underlying column; the
specific value is excluded from the org schema and never crosses the
schema boundary on any surface projecting through this base class.
Consumer subclass re-declares the value field so a consumer viewing
their own record still sees what they set.

CheckCancelledPayload.description:
Fired when a check transitions to the CANCELLED terminal state.

Sole dispatcher: ``services/check_service/lifecycle.py::cancel_check``.
The sandbox trigger's ``build_check_cancelled_payload`` at
``services/webhook_service.py`` produces byte-identical output.

Historically the allowlist admitted ``status`` and ``reason`` — the
dispatcher has never sent either (#836 documented this: "the
dispatcher today emits exactly two fields"). Dropped in #1048 as
dead promises.

``cancelled_at`` was previously ``None`` in production because
``cancel_check`` didn't stamp ``completed_at`` (only the ``status``
transition happened). #1059 fixed that — CANCELLED is a terminal
state, so ``completed_at`` is now stamped as part of the transition
and receivers get the real cancellation timestamp. Still typed as
optional because historical rows written before #1059 have
``completed_at`` = ``NULL`` and a re-dispatch (e.g., replay) would
still ship ``None`` for them.

Populated for cancellations recorded after #1059 (2026-08-17). ``None`` for the historical rows written before that, where the ``completed_at`` column was never stamped — receivers should treat those as ``event_timestamp - epsilon``.

certification_text_hash.description: Digest of the Gonos-published §1681b(b)(1)(A) End-User Certification for this purpose — a certification YOU, the requesting end user, make to Gonos. It is NOT a hash of your own wording, and NOT a consumer-facing disclosure: this text is never shown to the consumer. Fetch it from GET /api/v1/certifications/{permissible_purpose}, READ it — it binds you to purpose limitation, §1681b(b)(2) disclosure, §1681b(b)(3) adverse-action and EEO obligations — then send the `hash` field back verbatim. A digest of any other text is refused for purposes that have a published text. Required for 'employment' (§1681b(b)(1)(A)). Format: 'sha256:<hex>' or raw hex digest (SHA-256/384/512). The consumer's own clear-and-conspicuous disclosure and written authorization are a separate step, captured by the consent session (§1681b(b)(2)).

ConsentRevokedPayload.description:
Fired when a consumer revokes consent for a check.

Three dispatchers fire this event, all in
``services/consent/lifecycle.py``:

- ``revoke_consent`` (success path)
- the auto-expire-on-revoke branch (fires when revoke arrives on
  an already-expired consent)
- ``expire_due_consents`` (scheduled worker sweep)

All three call the shared assembler
:func:`gonos.services.webhook_service.assemble_consent_revoked_payload`
(#1049), so the wire shape is byte-identical across dispatchers.
Historically the three sent disjoint keys — the success path sent
``{consent_id, candidate_id, revoked_at}`` (no ``check_id``), the
auto-expire branch sent ``{consent_id, candidate_id, check_id,
revoked_at}``, and the scheduled sweep sent
``{consent_id, candidate_id, check_id, revoked_at, reason}`` with
``reason`` stripped by the allowlist.

Same anti-pattern #993 fixed for ``adverse_action.completed`` and
#1032 fixed for ``.cancelled``/``.reconsidered``.

candidate_id.description: ID of the candidate whose consent was revoked
candidate_id.title: Candidate Id

check_id.description: ID of the check the consent authorized. Non-optional — FCRA §1681b requires consent to name the check it authorizes, and all three dispatch paths have this value in scope. Newly delivered to receivers on the ``revoke_consent`` success path as of 2026-08-15 (previously omitted from that path's payload).
check_id.title: Check Id

idempotency_key.description: Deterministic dedup key of the form ``consent.revoked:<consent_id>``. Receivers can safely dedupe replays on this value. Matches the convention set by ``adverse_action.completed`` (#993) and ``.cancelled``/``.reconsidered`` (#1032).
idempotency_key.title: Idempotency Key

organization_id.description: ID of the organization that owns the resource
organization_id.title: Organization Id

reason.description: Reason the consent was revoked. Values in production: the caller-supplied string on user-initiated revocation (``None`` if the caller omitted it), ``'consent_expired'`` on the scheduled-expiry sweep, and any string the caller passed on the auto-expire-on-revoke cascade. Newly delivered to receivers on all paths as of 2026-08-15 (previously stripped by the allowlist even though the scheduled-sweep path sent it since inception; the other two paths did not pass it to the webhook until this change).
reason.title: Reason

revoked_at.description: ISO 8601 timestamp of when the revocation was recorded
revoked_at.title: Revoked At

timestamp.title: Timestamp

ConsumerReportSummarySchema.description:
The same summary, plus the fields only the consumer may see.

``extra="ignore"`` on the parent is what keeps internal summary keys off the
partner surface, and it is load-bearing — see the note above. The cost is
that it is audience-blind: a key added to the summary JSONB for the
*consumer's* benefit is dropped just as silently on the consumer's own
routes, which is not the same decision at all.

#992 hit exactly that. Court-erased records are withheld from the report,
and the relief that withheld them is named for the consumer but deliberately
not for the employer — telling the employer "excluded by expungement"
discloses the erasure the statutes exist to conceal. The relief-named list
was moved to a summary key on the reasoning that "undeclared on
``ReportSummarySchema`` + absent from ``CONSUMER_INTERNAL_SUMMARY_KEYS`` =
consumer-visible". The first half of that is right and the second is not:
``ConsumerReportResponse.summary`` was typed with the *partner* schema, so
the key reached only the CCPA/GDPR export and none of the three consumer
report routes. The consumer and the employer received identical text, which
is the one outcome the split existed to prevent.

So the consumer surface gets its own schema. Anything added here is visible
to the consumer and still invisible to the partner, which is the property
the JSONB-key convention was reaching for and could not express.

civil_records.title: Civil Records

consumer_disposition_factor_codes.title: Consumer Disposition Factor Codes

consumer_disposition_factors.description: CFPB Circular 2024-06 explanation of records withheld from this report, naming the specific legal relief (expungement, sealing) that withheld them. Consumer-facing only: the partner-facing summary carries a generic line instead, because naming the relief would disclose to the requesting organization the erasure that state statutes exist to conceal.
consumer_disposition_factors.title: Consumer Disposition Factors

disposition_factor_codes.description: Machine-readable form of ``disposition_factors`` (#1110 option 2). List of ``{code, count?, ...params}`` dicts naming the same set of factors the prose above renders in English. Consumer surfaces read these to render per-locale prose at read time; partner surfaces continue reading the English prose above for backwards compatibility.
disposition_factor_codes.title: Disposition Factor Codes

disposition_factors.description: Factors that contributed to the report disposition. null means UNKNOWN, never 'no factors'. It is null on corrected reports (version > 1): the factors describe the filter run that produced the superseded version, and the correction paths lack the jurisdiction rules needed to rebuild them, so they are dropped rather than restated inaccurately.
disposition_factors.title: Disposition Factors

excluded_by_medical_debt.description: Records excluded per CFPB medical debt ban
excluded_by_medical_debt.title: Excluded By Medical Debt

It is absent on a report that predates the field, and on a corrected report (version > 1) whose path could not recompute the reasons — the expired-dispute sweep and the admin supersede route have no filter result, and create_corrected_report skips its recompute when the check has no items or the recompute raises. The column is encrypted at rest (ADR 0010/0012); a platform-scope audit copy of the same text is not, and is reachable only by CRA staff.

consumer_statement_unavailable.description: True when the consumer FILED a §1681i(b) statement and the CRA provably destroyed the value (ADR 0039 encryption-failure marker on write), so `consumer_statement` carries a placeholder -- an explanation on consumer-facing responses, the stable token on org-facing ones -- rather than the consumer's own words. That is a different state from the ordinary case of no statement at all, where `consumer_statement` is null. Clients gating an 'add a statement' control on `consumer_statement` being null must also treat this flag as null-equivalent, or they hide the control from the one consumer who needs it, and label this agency's placeholder as the consumer's own statement. It does NOT mean the words are gone from every copy: on the AMEND path the same transaction writes the plaintext to a platform-scope audit row, so the agency may still hold recoverable text. **Read `consumer_statement_unreadable` beside it** — this flag names the permanent loss, and the sibling names the recoverable one (a decrypt failure on valid ciphertext, which becomes False again once the key is restored).
consumer_statement_unavailable.title: Consumer Statement Unavailable

consumer_statement_unreadable.description: True when the consumer FILED a §1681i(b) statement and the column carries valid ciphertext that will not decrypt **right now** -- key rotation, AAD drift, KMS outage -- so `consumer_statement` is null (fail-closed on read, #1937) but the raw column still holds the encrypted bytes. Distinct from `consumer_statement_unavailable` in permanence: this becomes False again once the key material is restored; that flag names a write-time destruction that never comes back. Distinct from `consumer_statement is null` in what remediation is possible: 'never filed' has nothing to recover; this row has recoverable ciphertext. Clients gating an 'add a statement' control on `consumer_statement` being null must treat this flag as null-equivalent, same as `consumer_statement_unavailable` — a re-file would silently discard the recoverable text. This flag was False on every row before #2075; #2075 filed it. The two flags are mutually exclusive: a row cannot both hold the marker (which decrypts cleanly) AND be undecryptable.
consumer_statement_unreadable.title: Consumer Statement Unreadable

the headline deadlines) for a consistent, lightweight list payload across
resources. Fetch the dispute detail endpoint for the full record, including

consumer_statement_unreadable.description: True when the consumer FILED a §1681i(b) statement and the column carries valid ciphertext that will not decrypt **right now** -- key rotation, AAD drift, KMS outage -- so `consumer_statement` is null (fail-closed on read, #1937) but the raw column still holds the encrypted bytes. Distinct from `consumer_statement_unavailable` in permanence: this becomes False again once the key material is restored; that flag names a write-time destruction that never comes back. Distinct from `consumer_statement is null` in what remediation is possible: 'never filed' has nothing to recover; this row has recoverable ciphertext. Clients gating an 'add a statement' control on `consumer_statement` being null must treat this flag as null-equivalent, same as `consumer_statement_unavailable` — a re-file would silently discard the recoverable text. This flag was False on every row before #2075; #2075 filed it. The two flags are mutually exclusive: a row cannot both hold the marker (which decrypts cleanly) AND be undecryptable.

ErrorResponse.description:
Standard error response body returned for all 4xx/5xx responses.

R69-H8: `detail` is always a human-readable string. Field-level validation
errors (from RequestValidationError) are returned in a separate `errors` key
to keep the type consistent for SDK generation.

**Two error identifiers, two distinct contracts (M-8 audit fix):**

The response carries both ``error`` and ``error_code`` because they serve
different consumers and have different stability guarantees:

* ``error`` — **always present** on every 4xx/5xx response. Lower-case
  ``snake_case`` slug derived from the HTTP failure class
  (``"not_found"``, ``"validation_error"``, ``"authentication_failed"``,
  ``"rate_limit_exceeded"``, ``"internal_error"``, …). Stable across
  releases. Safe for log indexing, dashboards, and generic client
  branching (``if body["error"] == "not_found": ...``).

* ``error_code`` — **domain-specific UPPER_SNAKE constant** raised by a
  specific business rule (``CONSENT_REQUIRED``,
  ``SECURITY_FREEZE_ACTIVE``, ``DPPA_PURPOSE_REQUIRED``, …). Always
  present on 4xx (and 503) responses, but **may be ``null`` on raw 500
  errors** because unhandled exceptions don't carry a domain code.
  Use this for programmatic handling of specific business outcomes.

Rule of thumb: branch on ``error`` for transport-level failures
(retry, refresh auth, 404 vs 422); branch on ``error_code`` for
business-rule failures that need a remediation flow.

**Guaranteed fields per HTTP status:**

=====  ===========  ======  ==========  ======  ==============
Status error        detail  error_code  errors  fix_suggestion
=====  ===========  ======  ==========  ======  ==============
400    always       always  always      yes*    sometimes
401    always       always  always      no      always
403    always       always  always      no      always
404    always       always  always      no      always
409    always       always  always      no      sometimes
412    always       always  always      no      sometimes
422    always       always  always      yes     sometimes
429    always       always  always      no      always
500    always       generic no          no      no
503    always       always  always      no      always
=====  ===========  ======  ==========  ======  ==============

(*) ``errors`` on 400/422 contains field-level validation detail.

The full set of ``error_code`` values is large and grows with each new
business rule, so it is not duplicated here (a hand-maintained list
rots). The canonical, always-current catalog is served by
``GET /api/v1/errors`` — fetch it for the complete enumeration plus
per-code descriptions and remediation hints.

correlation_id.description: Request correlation ID — always present on every error response
correlation_id.title: Correlation Id

error.description: Stable lower_snake_case transport-level error slug. Always present on every 4xx/5xx response. Branch on this for generic retry/auth/404 logic. See class docstring for the contract vs error_code.
error.title: Error

error_code.description: Domain-specific UPPER_SNAKE_CASE business-rule code for programmatic remediation flows (e.g. CONSENT_REQUIRED). Always present on 4xx, may be null on raw 500. See class docstring for the contract vs `error`.
error_code.title: Error Code

errors.description: Field-level validation errors (only present for 400 validation failures)

fix_suggestion.description: Suggested fix for this error — designed for AI coding assistants to auto-resolve common issues

resource_type.title: Resource Type

FreeDisclosureClaimRequest.description:
Audit-round-10 free disclosure claim body.

These are **§1681j(c)** entitlements, plus §1681j(d) for the fraud-alert
type — not §1681j(a)(1)(B)–(D), which this docstring and
``docs/COMPLIANCE.md`` both used to cite. §1681j(a)(1) is the *annual*
free disclosure and its (B)–(D) subparagraphs concern the centralised
request source, not additional entitlements. Same class of error as the
§1681j(b)/(d) swap swept in #1030; §1681j(c) was cited nowhere in the
repo before this.

Consumers are entitled to a free file disclosure beyond the annual one
(already served by ``/consumer/annual-disclosure``) when they:

* are unemployed and seeking work within 60 days — §1681j(c)(1),
* receive public welfare assistance — §1681j(c)(2),
* have reason to believe the file contains fraud-caused inaccuracy —
  §1681j(c)(3), or
* have placed a fraud alert / identity-theft block — §1681j(d), via
  §1681c-1(a)(2) and (b)(2).

Each entitlement is 1-per-12-month per type and requires the
consumer to attest. ``unemployment`` / ``public_assistance`` /
``fraud_victim`` additionally require supporting evidence (S3 key
references to documentation); ``identity_theft`` does not — an
active ``IdentityTheftBlock`` (§1681c-2) **or an active fraud
alert** (§1681c-1) is itself the evidence, matching the two triggers
this entitlement is described by above. An ordinary security freeze
is a different §1681c-1 right and does not qualify. The route
refuses with ``NO_ACTIVE_IDENTITY_THEFT_BLOCK`` when neither is
present. This
paragraph previously said every type required evidence, which
contradicted the ``evidence_storage_keys`` description below and
overstated what a consumer must supply — the direction that costs
someone an entitlement they are owed. It is published verbatim into
``openapi.json``, so a portal generated from this schema marked the
field mandatory for a type that does not need it.

The audit row is the entitlement consumption record — no separate
table.

FurnisherAgreementSignRequest.description:
#10: ESIGN-Act-style request body for signing the furnisher agreement.

Captures the four ESIGN elements: intent to sign (the boolean +
typed name), identification (name + title + email), what was
agreed to (text_hash), and the system-side authentication
(timestamp + IP + user agent come from request context).

agreement_text_hash.description: SHA-256 hex digest of the exact agreement text shown to the signer. Stored so we can prove what they agreed to under audit. Mismatch with the current published agreement means the signer saw stale terms — re-sign required.
agreement_text_hash.title: Agreement Text Hash

agreement_version.description: Semver of the agreement the signer saw.
agreement_version.title: Agreement Version

authority_to_bind.description: ADR 0122: capacity-to-bind hardening — named by the ADR as the sharpest B2B click-through attack vector. The signer attests separately from ``intent_to_sign`` that they have authority to bind the organization to the agreement; intent-to-sign alone can be a signer who meant to sign but had no authority to. The server rejects False and persists the value in the signing-audit row so the attestation is readable from the audit trail. Submitting False or omitting the field rejects the request — unattested authority is the shape this hardening exists to catch.
authority_to_bind.title: Authority To Bind

intent_to_sign.description: Affirms ESIGN-Act intent: 'I intend to electronically sign this agreement and understand it is legally binding.' Required — submitting False rejects the request.
intent_to_sign.title: Intent To Sign

scrolled_to_bottom.description: ADR 0122: §1681e(a) read-evidence hardening. The client sets this true after the user has actually scrolled the agreement body to the bottom (the UI disables the sign button until then). The server rejects False and persists the value in the signing-audit row so a CFPB examiner can read the attestation from the audit trail, not just the wire. Submitting False or omitting the field rejects the request — an unread agreement is the shape this hardening exists to catch.
scrolled_to_bottom.title: Scrolled To Bottom

signer_email.title: Signer Email

signer_name.description: Full legal name of the signer (typed as signature).
signer_name.title: Signer Name

IdentityLockoutCompliance.description:
Consumers who cannot pass the §1681g identity gate on the CRA's own row.

These consumers are refused *while supplying correct credentials*, because
the stored operand is absent, unusable, or undecryptable — so this is CRA
data quality, not consumer error, and the tenant holding `candidates:write`
is the party who can repair it via `PATCH /api/v1/candidates/{id}`.

**Read from a nightly snapshot, not computed live.** ADR 0026: the
classifier must DECRYPT, and with `kms_enabled=False` that is PBKDF2 at
600,000 iterations over a per-value salt, ~300-550ms per candidate. The
cost is inseparable from the security property, so it cannot be optimised
away — hence `taken_at`, and hence this section can be absent.

**The number sizes a POPULATION. It must never be used to decide whether a
PARTICULAR consumer is locked out** — that answer lives in the gate itself,
computed live at the moment it refuses. ADR 0026 names misuse of this
number for an individual as the observable that would mean the whole
persist-don't-compute decision was wrong.

by_cause.description: Breakdown of `cannot_pass_gate` only; healthy rows are not included, so these values sum to `cannot_pass_gate` and NOT to `candidates_scanned`. Keys are the classifier's cause names, so a new cause can appear without an API change — read the map rather than switching on a fixed key set. Current keys, NOT exhaustive: `identity_not_on_file` — an operand was never stored; collect the value from the consumer and PATCH the candidate. `stored_value_unusable` — an operand is stored but cannot match any admissible input; PATCH the candidate. `unknown` — the stored value cannot be decrypted. This is a fault on OUR side, not yours: do NOT overwrite it, because that destroys the evidence of a key problem which may affect many rows at once. Report it. Per ADR 0023 these consumers also have no knowledge-based substitute, so they are the most urgent group and the one you cannot resolve alone. Example: {"identity_not_on_file": 4, "unknown": 1}.
by_cause.title: By Cause

candidates_scanned.description: Candidates walked in that run — the denominator. Not revised by later retention purges, so it is an as-of figure.
candidates_scanned.title: Candidates Scanned

cannot_pass_gate.description: Consumers blocked AS OF `taken_at` whose files still exist. Repairs you make are NOT reflected until the next snapshot, so a falling number between snapshots means files were deleted under retention, not that anyone was repaired. Do not divide this by `candidates_scanned`: the two have different as-of semantics. `GET /api/v1/compliance/identity-lockouts` returns the consumers behind this number, from the same snapshot and the same `taken_at`.
cannot_pass_gate.title: Cannot Pass Gate

taken_at.description: When the snapshot this section reports was taken. Coverage rotates over nights (ADR 0027), so this can legitimately be several days old on a large platform.
taken_at.title: Taken At

IdentityLockoutCompliance.title: IdentityLockoutCompliance

IdentityLockoutItem.description:
One consumer who could not pass the identity gate, as of the snapshot.

Carries the candidate id so the tenant can act, and the cause so they know
WHICH action — the three causes have three different remedies and one of
them is not theirs to perform.

candidate_id.description: Repair via `PATCH /api/v1/candidates/{candidate_id}` — except for cause `unknown`, which you must report rather than overwrite. There is no tenant-facing way to re-check ONE consumer live: the classifier runs inside the identity gate, which only the consumer can trigger. So do not wait for a fresher verdict — PATCH the operand regardless of whether you believe the row is current. PATCHing an already-repaired candidate is harmless.
candidate_id.title: Candidate Id

cause.description: Why this consumer was blocked at `taken_at`. `identity_not_on_file` — an operand was never stored; collect it from the consumer and PATCH. `stored_value_unusable` — stored but unmatchable; PATCH. `unknown` — the stored value cannot be decrypted. OUR fault, not yours: report it, do NOT overwrite, because overwriting destroys the evidence of a key problem that may affect many rows at once. Not an exhaustive set — a new cause can appear without an API change, so do not switch on a fixed key set.
cause.title: Cause

IdentityLockoutItem.title: IdentityLockoutItem

IdentityLockoutListResponse.description:
The consumers behind the dashboard's `cannot_pass_gate` count.

**This list must not be used as a factor in any hiring, retention or
eligibility decision.** A consumer appears here because the CRA cannot
identify them against its own stored row — it is a defect in OUR record,
not a finding about the person, and it says nothing whatever about their
history. Acting on it adversely would deny someone on the strength of a
CRA data fault while bypassing the §1681m adverse-action notice they would
have received had the same decision come from their report. It would also
fall hardest on the group least able to answer it: these consumers are, by
construction, the ones who cannot pass the §1681g gate to obtain their file
or open a §1681i dispute.

The one sound use is repair: PATCH the operands the two tenant-repairable
causes name, and escalate `unknown` to the CRA.

snapshot.description: **null means this organization has not been measured** — which is NOT the same as having no blocked consumers. A non-null value with `total: 0` genuinely means nobody was blocked at its `taken_at`. See the `identity_lockout` section of `GET /compliance/dashboard`, which reports the same snapshot as a count.

IdentityLockoutListResponse.title: IdentityLockoutListResponse

IdentityLockoutSnapshotPage.description:
One page of a snapshot that EXISTS. Absent entirely when none does.

Inherits the platform's standard pagination envelope (`items`, `total`,
`page`, `per_page`, `pages`, `has_next`, `has_prev`) and adds the one field
that makes this list different from every other list in the API: the date
the answer was true.

**This is an AS-OF list, not a live one, and the distinction matters before
you contact anyone.** The verdicts were computed at `taken_at`; a consumer
you repaired since then is still listed, because nothing re-runs the
classifier between snapshots. Treat a row as "was blocked at `taken_at`",
never as "is locked out now".

That caveat is the whole reason this is a separate endpoint rather than a
section on `/analytics/action-items`: every row on that surface is live SQL
over current state, and a snapshot row sitting among them would inherit a
currency it does not have.

Why the staleness cannot be engineered away: deciding the cause requires
DECRYPTING the stored operand, and with KMS disabled that is PBKDF2 at
600,000 iterations over a per-value salt — the cost is inseparable from the
security property (ADR 0026). The live answer for one consumer exists only
inside the identity gate, at the moment it refuses them.

taken_at.description: When these verdicts were computed. Repairs you have made since are NOT reflected. Coverage rotates over nights (ADR 0027), so this can be several nights old on a large platform.
taken_at.title: Taken At

total.description: Total number of items across all pages
total.title: Total

IdentityLockoutSnapshotPage.title: IdentityLockoutSnapshotPage

OnboardingTrack.description:
Which setup path an organization is actually walking.

The checklist used to be a single flat list of seven steps, four of
which (API key, sandbox run, webhook, "run your first check via the
API") only exist for integrators. A CRA that runs every check from the
admin portal — a real and common shape here — could reach 3/7 and stop,
with the two obligations that actually gate them (the furnisher
agreement and the §1681b(f) end-user certification) ranked below setup
work they will never do.

Membership decides only which steps count toward progress. Nothing is
hidden or forbidden: a PORTAL org can still mint an API key, and the
steps outside its track are returned with ``applicable=False`` so the
UI can offer them without dragging down the denominator.
OnboardingTrack.title: OnboardingTrack

OnboardingTrackSource.description:
Whether the org's track was chosen by a human or inferred.

INFERRED is the default and is recomputed on every read, so an org that
mints its first API key moves to the API track without anyone touching
a setting. Once someone picks a track explicitly the choice is SELECTED
and inference stops — otherwise a portal-only org that minted one key
for a spike would be dragged back to the API track forever.
OnboardingTrackSource.title: OnboardingTrackSource

OrgApplicationPublicResponse.description:
Response returned to the public applicant — no internal review fields.

``status`` is the raw enum value (e.g. ``"under_review"``).
``status_display`` is the human-readable label via ``DisplayNameMixin``
so applicants can render the status without a hardcoded translation.

#12: ``status_token`` is a signed JWT that grants the applicant
read access to this one application's status via
``GET /public/applications/{id}?token=...``. Subsequent status lookups
don't re-issue the token.

#1674: ``status_url`` is **deprecated and always null**. It was built as
``{frontend_base_url}/applications/{id}/status?token=...`` and documented
here as a link to email verbatim, at a time when the frontend served no
such route — so the sentence was an instruction to send applicants a 404.
Nothing had written that email yet, which is the only reason no one
received one.

#1696 has since built that route, so the 404 is gone. The field stays
null anyway, and for a different reason: composing an applicant-facing URL
is the frontend's job, and reviving a server-built one would put that
routing back in the API's hands. The field stays declared until
``x-removed-in`` so an SDK deserialising it does not break (the Selky
``ttl_hours`` incident, ``docs/SCHEMA_EVOLUTION.md``); the pair to build a
link from is ``id`` + ``status_token``.

status_display.description: Human-readable label for status, suitable for display.
status_display.title: Status Display

status_token.description: Signed token granting status-lookup access. Only returned on POST (the original submit response). Re-fetches do not re-issue.
status_token.title: Status Token

status_url.description: Deprecated and always null (#1674). Compose the link yourself from `id` and `status_token`: /applications/{id}/status?token=... is the route the site serves (#1696). This field stays null because building an applicant-facing URL belongs to the frontend, not the API.
status_url.title: Status Url

OrgDisputeExtensionResponse.description:
The org-facing twin of `DisputeExtensionResponse`.

Inherits from `OrgDisputeResponse`, NOT from `DisputeExtensionResponse`:
the org model exists to withhold the consumer's own explanation of why they
needed more time (#1606), and inheriting from the consumer model would put
that back on the exact route it leaked from.

Both audiences get the grant. An organization that asked for 15 days and was
given 5 has the same reason to know as a consumer does, and this service
computes one number for both.

consumer_statement.title: Consumer Statement

consumer_statement_unavailable.description: True when the consumer FILED a §1681i(b) statement and the CRA provably destroyed the value (ADR 0039 encryption-failure marker on write), so `consumer_statement` carries a placeholder -- an explanation on consumer-facing responses, the stable token on org-facing ones -- rather than the consumer's own words. That is a different state from the ordinary case of no statement at all, where `consumer_statement` is null. Clients gating an 'add a statement' control on `consumer_statement` being null must also treat this flag as null-equivalent, or they hide the control from the one consumer who needs it, and label this agency's placeholder as the consumer's own statement. It does NOT mean the words are gone from every copy: on the AMEND path the same transaction writes the plaintext to a platform-scope audit row, so the agency may still hold recoverable text. **Read `consumer_statement_unreadable` beside it** — this flag names the permanent loss, and the sibling names the recoverable one (a decrypt failure on valid ciphertext, which becomes False again once the key is restored).
consumer_statement_unavailable.title: Consumer Statement Unavailable

consumer_statement_unreadable.description: True when the consumer FILED a §1681i(b) statement and the column carries valid ciphertext that will not decrypt **right now** -- key rotation, AAD drift, KMS outage -- so `consumer_statement` is null (fail-closed on read, #1937) but the raw column still holds the encrypted bytes. Distinct from `consumer_statement_unavailable` in permanence: this becomes False again once the key material is restored; that flag names a write-time destruction that never comes back. Distinct from `consumer_statement is null` in what remediation is possible: 'never filed' has nothing to recover; this row has recoverable ciphertext. Clients gating an 'add a statement' control on `consumer_statement` being null must treat this flag as null-equivalent, same as `consumer_statement_unavailable` — a re-file would silently discard the recoverable text. This flag was False on every row before #2075; #2075 filed it. The two flags are mutually exclusive: a row cannot both hold the marker (which decrypts cleanly) AND be undecryptable.
consumer_statement_unreadable.title: Consumer Statement Unreadable

So null means 'no category recorded OR a category not shown to you', and must never be read as 'an ordinary extension'.

ReinvestigationArtifact.description:
One re-fetch of one disputed CheckItem against its original data source.

§1681i(a)(1)(A) evidence: this is what the CRA actually looked at when it
re-checked the disputed finding. ``new_payload`` is deliberately NOT
exposed here — it is a PII blob, and the audit-relevant parts (the hashes
and the computed diff) are sufficient to show the comparison was made.

The evidence of the re-check is this artifact itself: ``source``,
``fetched_at``, ``fetch_status``, ``diff_summary`` and the two hashes.
``new_payload`` is encrypted at rest for artifacts written on or after
2026-09-04; rows written before that are still plaintext pending a
backfill. No endpoint returns it in either case, and there is no
partner-facing decryption path.

Known limitation: ``comparison_result`` currently reports ``differs`` for
every successful re-fetch, including one whose source data is unchanged.
``matches`` is not produced today.

check_item_id.description: The disputed check item that was re-fetched
check_item_id.title: Check Item Id

comparison_result.description: Comparison against the original record: 'matches' (verifies the original), 'differs' (forces the corrected resolution path), 'unverifiable' (source unreachable), or 'pending'
comparison_result.title: Comparison Result

created_at.description: When the artifact row was written
created_at.title: Created At

diff_summary.description: Compact human-readable diff (keys added/removed, record_count delta)
diff_summary.title: Diff Summary

fetch_status.description: Outcome of the re-fetch: 'success' (new payload stored), 'error' (non-transient client error), 'unreachable' (retried and gave up — §1681i(a)(5)(A)(i) deletion path), or 'skipped'
fetch_status.title: Fetch Status

fetched_at.description: Wall-clock time of the external API call
fetched_at.title: Fetched At

new_payload_hash.description: SHA-256 of the freshly fetched record as fetched, in canonical JSON (sorted keys). This is a digest of the PLAINTEXT payload, not of the encrypted value stored beside it — hashing the ciphertext would verify nothing, because the encryption uses a random IV and the digest would differ on every write. To reproduce: decrypt, parse, re-serialize with sorted keys, then SHA-256.
new_payload_hash.title: New Payload Hash

original_payload_hash.description: SHA-256 of the original record at artifact creation
original_payload_hash.title: Original Payload Hash

source.description: Data source re-queried, snapshotted at fetch time
source.title: Source

Fired when a security freeze is permanently lifted.

Two dispatchers as of #2102:
- ``services/freeze_service.py::lift_freeze`` — consumer-initiated,
  via the /consumer/freeze/{id}/lift route with the consumer's PIN.
- ``api/v1/admin/freezes.py::admin_lift_freeze`` — platform-initiated

info.description:
FCRA-compliant background verification API for platforms. Provides criminal records, identity verification, credit reports, motor vehicle records, drug testing, and continuous monitoring.

## Quick Start
1. Create a candidate: `POST /api/v1/candidates`
2. Create a check: `POST /api/v1/checks` with package and permissible purpose
3. Capture consent and submit: `POST /api/v1/checks/{id}/submit`
4. Receive results via webhook or poll `GET /api/v1/checks/{id}/report`

## Authentication
All endpoints require `X-API-Key` header. Consumer portal uses JWT Bearer tokens.

## Sandbox
Use candidate last name prefixes `SandboxClear`, `SandboxHit`, etc. for testing.

## SCIM 2.0
SCIM user provisioning endpoints are mounted at `/scim/v2/`. See [RFC 7644](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7644) for the SCIM protocol. SCIM endpoints use `application/scim+json` content type and Bearer token auth.

## Terminology

- **Candidate**: Person undergoing a background check (created by platform via API)
- **Consumer**: The same person when exercising FCRA rights (viewing reports, filing disputes via consumer portal)
- **User**: Platform admin/staff member (portal access, manages organization settings)
- **Organization (Org)**: The platform/company using Gonos to run background checks

## Rate Limits
All endpoints are rate-limited per client IP. Services sharing an egress IP (NAT gateway, corporate proxy) share one bucket — size your traffic accordingly or contact us for a dedicated allocation. Per-route baselines:

| Category | Limit | Applies to |
|----------|-------|------------|
| **auth** | 10 rpm | Login, register, magic link |
| **consumer** | 60 rpm | `/consumer/*` portal endpoints |
| **platform** | 120 rpm | All other endpoints (default) |

Rate-limited responses return `429` with `Retry-After`, `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, and `X-RateLimit-Reset` headers.

## Timestamps
All timestamps are in ISO 8601 format with UTC timezone (`Z` suffix). Example: `2026-03-01T12:00:00Z`.

## Error Handling
All errors return a consistent JSON shape:
```json
{"error": "...", "detail": "...", "error_code": "...", "kind": "user|retryable|ops", "correlation_id": "...", "errors": [], "fix_suggestion": "..."}
```
### `kind` — how to route an error without a code table
`kind` is a stable, three-valued classification carried on every error. Branch on it instead of on HTTP status or on a list of `error_code` values you have to keep in sync:

| `kind` | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `user` | Safe to display to an end user; describes something they can fix | Surface `detail` (and `errors[]`) in your UI |
| `retryable` | Transient | Retry with backoff |
| `ops` | Your team must act — credentials, scopes, plan limits, bugs | Alert; never show `detail` to an end user |

New error codes are always born into one of these three, so a code you have never seen cannot fall through to raw exposure. Unrecognized values should be treated as `ops`.

Use `GET /api/v1/errors` for the full error code catalog with descriptions and HTTP statuses. Each endpoint includes `x-error-codes` in its OpenAPI extensions mapping HTTP status codes to the specific error codes it may return — SDK generators can use this to auto-document error handling per operation.

## Idempotency
Endpoints marked `x-idempotent: true` accept an `Idempotency-Key` header (UUID). Keys are scoped per endpoint: the same key on a different endpoint is an independent key. Retrying the identical request within 24h returns the cached response with `Idempotency-Replayed: true`; reusing a key on the same endpoint with a different request returns 422 `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED`. Mint one key per distinct request, not one per logical job.

post.description:
H9: Reconsider an adverse action in favor of the consumer.

**Reconsideration workflow:**

1. The platform calls this endpoint when new information (e.g., dispute
   resolution, candidate-provided context, or internal policy review)
   warrants reversing the adverse decision.
2. The adverse action transitions to ``reconsidered`` status, which is
   a terminal state — no further state changes are allowed.
3. An ``adverse_action.reconsidered`` webhook event is dispatched so
   downstream systems can update their records (e.g., rescind denial,
   restore candidate eligibility).
4. An audit trail entry is created with the ``reconsideration_reason``
   (if provided) for FCRA compliance documentation.

**When to use:** Call this endpoint instead of ``/finalize`` when the
platform decides *not* to proceed with the adverse action after the
pre-notice waiting period. This is distinct from ``/cancel`` (used
before or during the waiting period) and ``/withdraw`` (used before
the pre-notice is sent).

**Allowed source statuses:** ``pre_notice_sent`` (after waiting period).

Optionally accepts a body with ``reconsideration_reason`` for the audit
trail. Providing a reason is strongly recommended for compliance.

**Required scope:** `adverse_actions:write`

post.description:
M4 (§1681m(a)): re-send the pre-adverse notice after a failed delivery.

When the original pre-notice bounced or was dropped, the consumer never
received it. This endpoint queues a fresh pre-notice and resets the
5-business-day waiting period clock to anchor on the new send time —
preserving the consumer's full statutory window from the first day they
can act on the notice.

Requires the prior delivery to have a terminal failure state
(``bounced``/``failed``). For deliveries that never confirmed but didn't
fail, use ``/finalize`` with ``delivery_override_reason`` instead.

**Idempotency (ADR 0109):** Pass an `Idempotency-Key` header (UUID) so
a 502-retry does not reset the §1681m(a) waiting-period clock twice.
Keys expire after 24 hours.

**Required scope:** `adverse_actions:write`

post.description:
Close the loop on a correction to the report an adverse action rests on.

Which corrections count is decided by report version, not by when the final
notice went out: an action is queued when the denial rests on a version
below the corrected one, so a correction that landed before the notice cycle
began still counts. The final notice remains a precondition for eligibility
at all — only actions in `final_sent` or `completed` can reach this endpoint,
because earlier ones are cancelled outright when a correction lands.

When a dispute resolves as corrected, adverse actions still awaiting their
final notice are cancelled automatically. Ones already notified cannot be:
the status machine offers no path out of `final_sent` / `completed`. Those
appear under `adverse_actions_pending_correction_review` in
`GET /analytics/action-items` and in the daily digest until this endpoint
is called.

Recording a resolution does **not** reverse the adverse action or notify
the consumer — reversing it is the employer's decision under §1681m(a).
It records that the org reviewed the case, which is what takes it off the
queue.

**Required scope:** `adverse_actions:write`

Return the canonical launch tiers with their live prices + compositions.

Unauthenticated public endpoint. Homepage / pricing page / dashboard /
SDK / CLI / AI docs should all derive from here rather than
independently hardcoding prices or compositions — the plan's "one
authoritative catalog" step.

  ``price_cents`` per package) — changes when ops seeds a new catalog.

  ``turnaround_hours``, ``pass_through_fees``,

in the response. Aliases (``essential``, ``staffing``, etc.) are
accepted by ``POST /checks`` but not advertised here — they're
back-compat, not products. ``sandbox_demo`` is an operator-only probe
path and never surfaces.

get.description:
Which purposes have canonical §1681b(f) text, and each one's hash.

Declared before ``/{purpose}`` so the empty path is not captured by the
path parameter.

Exists because the set is not a constant anyone can safely hard-code.
Since ADR 0024 a certification authorises only the purpose it names, so
"which purposes can I certify?" is a question with a real answer that
changes when Gonos publishes a new text (#1817) — and a client holding a
stale copy of the list would hide a purpose that had become available.
The admin portal's certification form reads this rather than embedding a
list of its own.

Unauthenticated for the same reason as the detail route: the text has to be
readable by whoever signs it before an API key exists. It is the
INTEGRATOR's certification to Gonos and is not shown to the consumer --
their own disclosure and authorization are the separate consent session
(§1681b(b)(2)).

get.description:
Pre-flight ``(package, permissible_purpose)`` validation for #381.

Answers "will ``POST /checks`` reject this combination?" without
actually POSTing anything or burning quota. Always returns 200; the
``valid`` flag in the body says whether the config passes the
synchronous rules.

**What this covers.** All synchronous, side-effect-free rules that
``POST /checks`` (and ``POST /checks/{id}/submit``) apply:

- purpose is a recognised FCRA §1681b(a) value
- purpose is in the org's ``allowed_purposes`` (when configured)
- package/purpose compatibility per §1681b(a)(3)
- ``insurance`` purpose requires ``insurance_subtype``

**What this does NOT cover.** Consent lifecycle, freezes / fraud
alerts, identity-theft blocks, certification-text-hash presence,
retention windows, quota, sandbox-vs-live gating. A response with
``valid: true`` says the config is compatible — a subsequent
``POST /checks`` can still fail on any of those.

**Required scope:** ``checks:read``.

get.description:
The consumers behind `identity_lockout.cannot_pass_gate` on the dashboard.

**Do not use this list as a factor in any hiring, retention or eligibility
decision.** A consumer is listed because this CRA cannot identify them
against its own stored row. That is a defect in OUR record, not a finding
about the person, and it carries no information about their history. A
decision made on it would deny someone over a CRA data fault while
bypassing the §1681m adverse-action notice they would have received had the
same decision come from their report — and it would land on the one group
least able to answer back, since these consumers cannot pass §1681g to
obtain their file or open a §1681i dispute.

**As-of, not live.** These verdicts were computed at `snapshot.taken_at`; a
consumer you have repaired since is still listed, because nothing re-runs
the classifier between snapshots. There is no tenant-facing way to re-check
one consumer — the classifier runs inside the identity gate, which only the
consumer can trigger — so the sound action is to PATCH the operand named by
the cause regardless of whether you think the row is current. PATCHing an
already-repaired candidate is harmless.

`snapshot: null` means this organization has not been measured, which is
NOT the same as having no blocked consumers.

**Required scope:** ``analytics:read``

post.description:
§1681b(b): let a consumer withdraw their own authorization.

Self-service revocation closes the gap where consumers previously had to ask
an operator to revoke on their behalf. Requires identity verification
(X-Identity-SSN4 / X-Identity-DOB headers, §1681h(a)(1)) and only acts on a
consent that belongs to the authenticated consumer's own candidate profile.

The service layer enforces that only PENDING/SIGNED consents are revocable
and refuses while the associated check is mid-processing (409); it also emits
the ``consent.revoked`` webhook so the platform and any furnisher integration
are notified.

get.description:
Consumer right-to-access: export the platform's data on this consumer.

Collects personal info (decrypted), checks, reports, disputes, adverse actions,
consents, notifications, unsubscribe preferences, and audit access log.

#1119: every collection except ``unsubscribes`` and ``audit_access_log`` is
capped at 500 rows (``check_items`` at 1000), newest first. The response
schema names the per-field caps. Signalling that a cap bound is the
substantive follow-up on #1119; this docstring stops asserting "ALL"
while the query caps, which was wrong regardless of that decision.

Rate-limited to 1 request per 24 hours per consumer.

**§1681h(a)(1) identity verification** (#984): the payload is substantively
a §1681g file disclosure — personal info decrypted, reports, disputes,
adverse actions with the un-filtered credit_score_disclosure — so the
``X-Identity-SSN4`` + ``X-Identity-DOB`` gate the sibling ``/consumer/
file`` route requires applies here too. Prior to this fix the only check
was account linkage (``user.candidate_id is not None``), which a stolen
consumer JWT satisfies by definition. Whether a candidate-scoped JWT
alone constitutes "proper identification" under §1681h(a)(1) is the open
counsel question (``needs-legal-review`` on #984); adding the gate is
the safer failure direction pending that answer, since over-cautious
identity refusal is recoverable and under-cautious disclosure is not.

**Deliberately not** wired to consume the §1681j annual entitlement by
default. CCPA §1798.100 / GDPR Art. 20 are separate rights from FCRA §1681j;
the twin ``/consumer/file`` consumes the entitlement precisely because it is
that entitlement being exercised. This route is not. The consume/no-consume
decision remains open on #984 pending counsel — ADR 0047 (Provisional) and
CRA-FED-CD-003. Fallback wiring: setting
``data_export_consumes_1681j_entitlement=True`` enables the same annual
gate ``/consumer/file`` runs, so the pivot on a narrow counsel read is a
config flip rather than a code deploy.

post.description:
Submit a consumer data deletion request per CCPA or GDPR.

Pass ``request_type`` in the body to identify the regime (``ccpa`` by
default; ``gdpr`` for EU residents invoking Article 17 right to erasure).
Both regimes are subject to FCRA-mandated retention for active checks and
active disputes. NOT for adverse-action windows: this sentence claimed one
until #2229 and no such gate exists here or in the sweep behind it (#2216,
ADR 0080). The route that does gate on an adverse action is
``request_data_purge`` via ``assert_candidate_purgeable``, a different
pipeline.

**The provision cited here used to be Art. 17(3)(b), and this sentence
refuted itself:** it said 17(3)(b) permits the retention "because the
processing is required by Union/Member State law". The FCRA is US federal
law, so it is neither — the docstring stated the test and failed it in the
same clause. The provision that fits is **Art. 17(3)(e)** (establishment,
exercise or defence of legal claims), which pairs with §1681p's limitations
window, and on the CCPA side **§1798.145(d)**'s FCRA activity exemption.

Both of those are this repo's own reading and are **not counsel-approved** —
the question is open on `docs/legal/decisions/CRA-FED-PRIV-001.md` and #2206,
which is why the consumer-facing messages below assert no provision at all.

post.description:
Audit-round-10 §1681j(a) entitlement closure.

Previously the consumer-rights static text mentioned these
entitlements but no claim path existed. This endpoint:

1. Validates identity (SSN4 + DOB).
2. Validates the entitlement type and (where applicable) the
   supporting evidence keys.
3. Validates the consumer attestation.
4. Checks the audit log for any prior claim of the same
   entitlement type within the past 12 months. If one exists,
   refuses with ``ENTITLEMENT_ALREADY_CLAIMED`` (1-per-12-months
   per the statute).
5. Audits the claim with the entitlement type + evidence keys.
   The audit row IS the entitlement consumption record.
6. Assembles + returns the consumer file (same shape as
   ``/consumer/annual-disclosure``).

The annual entitlement (``/consumer/annual-disclosure``) is
independent — claiming an extra entitlement here does NOT consume
the annual window.

post.description:
Audit-round-9 consumer-portal H4 fix: §1681c-1(d) PIN reset.

The freeze confirmation email already promises a 5-business-day
replacement-PIN process. This endpoint kicks off that flow:

1. Identity verification (SSN4 + DOB).
2. Service generates a strong urlsafe token, stores its hash on
   the freeze with a 7-day expiry, and queues a LETTER notification
   containing the plaintext token.
3. Operator's mail integration sends the letter (out of scope).
4. Consumer returns to ``confirm-pin-reset`` with the token + new PIN.

The token is **not** returned in the API response — only delivered
by mail per §1681c-1(d).

post.description:
Mint a presigned PUT URL for a §1681c-2 supporting document.

Step 1 of the two-step upload the block request now requires. Until #1333
the consumer passed `identity_theft_report_key` and `identification_key` as
free strings that nothing resolved — no existence check, no ownership check
— so the documentary precondition §1681c-2(a)(2) rests on could be two
arbitrary characters, or another tenant's key.

The key is minted here, under an org/candidate prefix, and `request_block`
refuses anything outside it. Same two-step shape as dispute evidence.

This establishes provenance, not substance: the bytes behind the key are
still whatever the consumer uploaded. Whether they constitute an identity
theft report as §1681a(q)(4) defines one is the operator determination the
activation hold waits for.

post.description:
Audit-round-9 consumer-portal absence fix: logout-everywhere.

Sets ``user.tokens_revoked_after = now`` so every outstanding JWT
whose ``iat`` is at or before this moment is rejected by the
``get_current_user`` dep. No per-JTI tracking required — one
timestamp invalidates the entire token corpus across every device.
The current request's JTI is also explicitly revoked so the
immediate session is closed before the response returns.

consumers can correct identifying information. Previously the only
way to update an address/phone/email was through the platform admin
API, which is unreachable to the consumer.

SSN and DOB updates are deliberately excluded — those changes
affect downstream FCRA matching and need the full re-enrollment
flow with identity proof, not a quick PATCH.

Encrypts email/phone and the five address columns via the existing PII
encryption layer. ``address_country`` is a bare ISO-3166 alpha-2 code and
is the one address field the model does not treat as encrypted PII.

post.description:
M9: Consumer right-to-delete request.

Checks for active checks and active disputes — those two and no more. This
docstring said "adverse actions" until #2229 and the gate has never had one:
`erasure_request_block_selects` carries `ACTIVE_CHECKS` and `ACTIVE_DISPUTES`,
which are also this route's two published error codes. The sweep behind it
does not carry `non_terminal_adverse_action` either, so §1681m progress is
protected at neither end — ADR 0080's gap, sized by
`pre_notice_erasure_gap_preflight`, open on #2216.

Sets retention_expires_at and queues a confirmation notification.

post.description:
Record that the consumer requested a §1681i(a)(1)(B) extension.

This is an **org-typed** body on a `CurrentOrg` (org-API-key) route:
the organization records the consumer's request on behalf of the
consumer -- typically after receiving it out-of-band. The route DOES
NOT move `investigation_deadline`; it captures the request and
routes it to CRA staff for review. A CRA staff member then calls
`POST /admin/disputes/{id}/extend` (which DOES move the deadline)
if the request is approved.

An earlier version of this docstring called this "Consumer-initiated",
which was wrong on the wire: the consumer's own request path is
`POST /consumer/disputes/{id}/request-extension`. That framing
mislabelled the actor on a partner-audience route (#1615).

**Required scope:** `disputes:write`

schema.description:
Result callback body from a lab provider (49 CFR Part 40).

Added in #887. The route pulled all twelve of these fields out of a raw
dict via ``body.get(...)``, so nothing at the boundary checked a type and
``openapi.json`` could not describe the request body — integrators and the
SDK had nothing to generate from, on the endpoint that writes DOT
drug-test results.

Three deliberate choices, each of which would be a defect if reversed:

**Extras are allowed** (Pydantic's default, stated here so nobody
"tightens" it). Real provider callbacks carry vendor-specific fields, and
this repo's own webhook tests use four of the twelve. ``extra="forbid"``
would reject traffic that works today.

**``status`` is a plain string, not an enum.** The provider vocabulary
lives in ``drug_test_service._STATUS_MAP`` and is mapped there, raising
``UNKNOWN_PROVIDER_STATUS`` for anything unrecognised. Copying the set into
an enum here would give it a second home to drift from — and the service's
version is the one that decides the resulting state.

**This model is NOT used as a route body parameter.** The webhook verifies
an HMAC signature over the raw bytes *before* parsing. A body parameter
would make FastAPI validate first, so an unsigned caller sending a
malformed payload would get a field-level 422 describing the expected
shape instead of a signature rejection. The route calls
``model_validate`` explicitly, after the signature check, to keep that
ordering.

Download organization audit logs as CSV or JSON (max 10,000 rows).

**Required scope:** ``audit_logs:read``

Use ``format=json`` for machine-readable output with optional ``details``
and ``signature`` fields.  The ``X-Gonos-Export-Hash`` response header
contains a SHA-256 digest of the exported content for tamper evidence.

``X-Gonos-Export-Total`` gives the number of rows matching the filter and
``X-Gonos-Export-Truncated`` is ``true`` when that exceeds the 10,000-row
cap. Both are always present, so absence means an older server rather than
a complete export. Rows are ordered newest first, so a truncated export
omits the OLDEST rows in the window — narrow ``from_date``/``to_date``
rather than assuming what you received is the whole period.

post.description:
Submit an organization application for review.

No authentication required. The applicant agrees to the furnisher
agreement and terms of service as part of the submission. The
response only exposes a small subset of fields so the applicant can
poll for status without leaking internal review details.

#12: the response includes a signed ``status_token``. Subsequent calls
to ``GET /public/applications/{id}`` require the token as a ``?token=``
query param — knowing the id alone is no longer enough. The submit
response is the only place the token surfaces.

#1674: this used to say the notification service should email
``status_url``. At the time that field pointed at a frontend route the
app did not serve, so the instruction was to send the applicant a 404.
#1696 has since built that route (``/applications/{id}/status?token=``),
but the field stays deprecated and always null: composing an
applicant-facing URL belongs to the frontend. A link emailed to an
applicant must be composed from ``id`` + ``status_token``.

**Idempotency:** if an application with the same applicant email and
business name already exists in an active state (submitted,
kyb_pending, or under_review), the existing application is returned
instead of creating a new one. A fresh status_token is issued each
time (the old token is still valid until its TTL elapses).

The idempotency check runs *before* the per-IP rate limit, so a
user who hits a network blip on the first submit and retries
immediately gets their existing record back instead of a 429.
Genuinely new submissions still consume rate-limit budget.

429.description: Per-IP rate limit exceeded

503.description: Self-serve applications are closed until launch (#1784). Status polling on GET /public/applications/{id} is unaffected.

get.description:
Look up an application by id and return its public status.

#12: the application id alone is no longer enough — the matching
signed ``token`` query param (issued by the submit endpoint) must
accompany the request.

Token failure splits by kind, and this docstring used to claim both
were ``401``:

- **missing / malformed / expired** → ``401``, generic, so the
  response cannot be used to probe for valid application ids.
- **well formed but issued for a DIFFERENT application** → ``403``
  (``AuthorizationError`` below), which
  ``tests/test_api/test_applications.py`` has asserted all along.
  A caller that maps only ``401`` to "your link is dead" sends this
  one to a generic error screen with a retry button that can never
  succeed — which is exactly what the applicant status page did
  until #1696's review caught it.

post.description:
Create a candidate, a pending check, and a hosted consent session.

Returns the three ids plus `hosted_url` — redirect the candidate
there and Gonos handles disclosure, signature, and the FCRA paper
trail.

**Atomic.** All three rows are created in one transaction. If any
step fails, nothing is persisted — there is no partial state for you
to reconcile, and a retry is safe.

**The check is not submitted.** It is created `pending`. Consent must
be signed first (§1681b(b)(2)); submit it afterwards with
`POST /checks/{id}/submit`, or let your webhook on
`consent_session.completed` do it.

**`disclosure_type` is derived** from `permissible_purpose` — you do
not need to know that employment requires a standalone disclosure.

**`external_id` reuses.** If a candidate with that `external_id`
already exists in your organization, it is reused rather than
rejected, and `candidate_reused` says so.

**Required scope:** `candidates:write` and `checks:write` (both).

post.description:
Challenge the endpoint to prove it wants to receive Gonos events.

Gonos POSTs a signed ``endpoint.verification_challenge`` carrying a
single-use nonce. To pass, the receiver must echo that nonce back in
the **same response** — in the ``X-Gonos-Challenge`` header, as
``{"challenge": "<nonce>"}``, or as the bare string body. Anything else,
including a 2xx with no echo, leaves the endpoint unverified.

**This is not the same check as** ``POST /webhooks/{id}/test``. The test
ping sends ``X-Gonos-Ping: true``, which tells receivers they may skip
signature verification — so a 2xx to it proves only that the URL is
reachable and returns 200, which plenty of servers unrelated to the
integrator will do for an unexpected POST. Echoing a nonce is what
distinguishes "someone is listening" from "someone agreed to listen",
and that distinction is the whole control.

Verification is per-URL: editing ``url`` clears ``verified_at`` and the
endpoint must pass this challenge again.

**Required scope:** ``webhooks:write``

post.summary: Finalize adverse action after waiting period

post.description:
H9: Reconsider an adverse action in favor of the consumer.

**Reconsideration workflow:**

1. The platform calls this endpoint when new information (e.g., dispute
   resolution, candidate-provided context, or internal policy review)
   warrants reversing the adverse decision.
2. The adverse action transitions to ``reconsidered`` status, which is
   a terminal state — no further state changes are allowed.
3. An ``adverse_action.reconsidered`` webhook event is dispatched so
   downstream systems can update their records (e.g., rescind denial,
   restore candidate eligibility).
4. An audit trail entry is created with the ``reconsideration_reason``
   (if provided) for FCRA compliance documentation.

**When to use:** Call this endpoint instead of ``/finalize`` when the
platform decides *not* to proceed with the adverse action after the
pre-notice waiting period. This is distinct from ``/cancel`` (used
before or during the waiting period) and ``/withdraw`` (used before
the pre-notice is sent).

**Allowed source statuses:** ``pre_notice_sent`` (after waiting period).

Optionally accepts a body with ``reconsideration_reason`` for the audit
trail. Providing a reason is strongly recommended for compliance.

**Required scope:** `adverse_actions:write`

post.description:
M4 (§1681m(a)): re-send the pre-adverse notice after a failed delivery.

When the original pre-notice bounced or was dropped, the consumer never
received it. This endpoint queues a fresh pre-notice and resets the
5-business-day waiting period clock to anchor on the new send time —
preserving the consumer's full statutory window from the first day they
can act on the notice.

Requires the prior delivery to have a terminal failure state
(``bounced``/``failed``). For deliveries that never confirmed but didn't
fail, use ``/finalize`` with ``delivery_override_reason`` instead.

**Idempotency (ADR 0109):** Pass an `Idempotency-Key` header (UUID) so
a 502-retry does not reset the §1681m(a) waiting-period clock twice.
Keys expire after 24 hours.

**Required scope:** `adverse_actions:write`
